subject: Troubleshooting initial values for a multistate JS model

messages.author: 5ff906c2720491d5
messages.subject: Troubleshooting initial values for a multistate JS model
parts:
Hi everyone,

I am trying to run a multistate JS model, adapting the code from Kery and Schaub, BPA Book, section 10.3.2 with some modifications for my data of course. 

So I'm doing a seasonal survival analysis on a capture-recapture data.
My capture history includes individuals in the rows and seasons as occasions in the columns. 
There are 5 stages that can be observed, these are:
1 = observed as juvenile in postwet season - Jpost
2 = observed as juvenile in prewet season - Jpre
3 = observed as adult in postwet season - Apost
4 = observed as adult in prewet season - Apre
5 = not seen

My true states are: (which I used to create my true state initial values)
1 = not entered - NE
2 = juvenile in postwet season - Jpost
4 = juvenile in prewet season - Jpre
4 = adult in postwet season - Apost
5 = adult in prewet season - Apre
6 = dead

and the life cycle is:
NE -> Jpost -> Jpre -> Apost <-> Apre

There are several assumptions:
1) A juvenile becomes an adult after two seasons (occasions).
2) indivduals enter the population as Jpost only. Meaning, the not entered state can only become Jpost state once the individual enters the population.
3) since my occasions are seasonal, the individual has to change stages each season, so the transition rate is fixed to 1. 

Now my problem is that when I try to run my model, I am getting errors which I think is caused by my initial values, such as:
warning: problem initializing stochastic node z[34, 2]: logProb is -Inf.
warning: logProb of data node y[34, 2]: logProb is -Inf.

I have high suspicions that this might be caused of adding a dummy occasion for the estimating the removal entry probability (gamma) from the not entered state to Jpost state. Because of my assumption nr. 2, i think here my initial values gets confused. I tried several ways to go around it, even tried to not put a dummy occasion, but still got the error.

Also, I tried the exact same model with simulated data before, and it worked fine. That's why I think the model is correct. 
So, I thought maybe this list can help me solve this issue. I'd be appreciated.

Sorry for the long mail, I am attaching the code with a subsample of the data which can be used to replicate the errors. 

Thank you very much in advance.
Best,
Dilsad

messages.author: f116cbe5c604c988
messages.subject: Re: Troubleshooting initial values for a multistate JS model
parts:
Dilsad, great question, and thanks for providing a good description and clear and reproducible code.

Without doing a deep-dive to funny understand your model, and your use of dummy states, etc, the problem you're seeing is coming from individuals like, for example:

i <- 34   ## individual no. 34
model_js_model_samper_1$z[i, ]   ## the initial values for z
##  [1] 1 4 6 6 6 6 6 6 6 6 6

model_js_model_samper_1$logProb_z[i, ]  ## the log-density associated with each
##  [1]         NA       -Inf -0.4654124  0.0000000  0.0000000  0.0000000
##  [7]  0.0000000  0.0000000  0.0000000  0.0000000  0.0000000

The -Inf in position no. 2 is an example of the problem.  Here's why that's equal to -Inf.  The transition probability for z, going from t=1 to t=2, is:

t <- 2
model_js_model_samper_1$ps[1, i, t-1, 1:6]
## [1] 0.7124225 0.2875775 0.0000000 0.0000000 0.0000000 0.0000000

This has probability = 0 of transitioning to the next value of z=4.

From the warnings you're seeing, you'll also find this same problem for individuals #50, #51, #62, etc.

warning: problem initializing stochastic node z[50, 2]: logProb is -Inf.
warning: problem initializing stochastic node z[51, 2]: logProb is -Inf.
warning: problem initializing stochastic node z[62, 2]: logProb is -Inf.
warning: problem initializing stochastic node z[64, 2]: logProb is -Inf.
warning: problem initializing stochastic node z[65, 2]: logProb is -Inf.
warning: problem initializing stochastic node z[68, 2]: logProb is -Inf.
## etc.....

Does this help clear up what's happening?  It seems like the second (t=2) value of z=4 for many individuals is inconsistent (at least according to the transition probabilities in the ps matrix) with the initial (t=1) values of z=1.

I hope this helps get you going.  Good luck, Dilsad.

Cheers,
Daniel
